title: Minimum Number of Platforms
directAnswer: The answer is the maximum number of trains present at the station at any single instant. Sort the arrival times and departure times into two separate sorted arrays, then sweep them with two pointers: every time the next event is an arrival, a train comes in (platforms++); every time it's a departure, one leaves (platforms--). Track the running peak. Sorting dominates at O(n log n); the sweep is O(n).

remember.pattern: Sort arrivals and departures separately, two-pointer sweep, track peak overlap
rules: The answer is the **maximum simultaneous overlap** of the time intervals — not the total number of trains.
Sort arrivals and departures into **two independent** sorted arrays; you deliberately break the pairing between a train's own arrival and departure.
On a tie (`arr[i] == dep[j]`), decide whether a train can arrive the instant another leaves. The common convention is **arrival counts first** (needs its own platform), so use `arr[i] <= dep[j]`.
Only update the peak on an **arrival** — departures never raise the count.
It's the same idea as a sweep line / 'meeting rooms' overlap count.
whenToUse: Count the maximum number of overlapping intervals at any point in time
Resource sizing: how many rooms / platforms / servers handle peak concurrency
Events have a start and an end and you care about simultaneous activity
You can decouple starts from ends and process them in time order
antiSignals: You must keep each interval's start tied to its own end → don't decouple; use a different model
You need WHICH intervals overlap, not just how many → interval tree / sweep with IDs
Intervals are weighted and you optimise a sum → weighted interval scheduling DP
Times are tiny bounded integers → a difference array over time can beat sorting
remember.takeaway: Minimum Platforms is the overlap-count sweep in disguise: sort starts and ends separately, walk them in time order, and the running balance's peak is the answer. Decoupling each train's arrival from its departure is the move people miss — once you do, it's a clean two-pointer merge. Same engine as Meeting Rooms II.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reframe 'minimum platforms' as 'maximum simultaneous overlap', and realise you can sort arrivals and departures independently and sweep them, instead of comparing every pair of trains.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Keeping arrivals paired with their own departures, comparing every pair O(n²), or mishandling the arr == dep tie so two trains 'share' a platform that they actually can't.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say 'the answer is the peak concurrency, so I'll sort starts and ends separately and sweep — a balance that goes up on arrivals and down on departures'. Then nail the tie convention explicitly and connect it to Meeting Rooms II.

problemStatement:
You are given two arrays, `arr` and `dep`, of size `n`, where `arr[i]` and `dep[i]` are the arrival and departure times of the `i`-th train at a station (with `arr[i] ≤ dep[i]`). A platform can hold at most one train at a time, and a train occupies a platform for the whole closed interval `[arr[i], dep[i]]`.

Return the ***minimum number of platforms*** needed so that no train ever waits. By convention, if one train departs at the exact moment another arrives, they ***cannot*** share a platform.
constraints: Times are given in a comparable format (e.g. integers like 900 for 09:00, or minutes since midnight)
A train arriving exactly when another departs needs its own platform (arrival-first tie rule)
understanding: Each train is a closed time interval. A platform is busy for the whole interval, so the number of platforms you need at any instant equals the number of intervals covering that instant. The minimum number of platforms is therefore the maximum, over all instants, of how many intervals overlap — the peak concurrency. We find that peak by walking through arrival and departure events in time order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If a train departs at exactly the time another arrives, can they share a platform?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By the standard convention, no — the arriving train needs its own platform that instant. That's why the tie test is arr <= dep (arrival counted before that departure frees up).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the arrival and departure arrays already sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not necessarily. I sort each independently; that decoupling is the key step and it doesn't matter that a train's own arrival and departure end up in different positions.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do arrivals and departures pair up by index after sorting?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, and they don't need to. We only count how many trains are present, never which specific train — so breaking the pairing is safe.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can times wrap past midnight?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll assume all times are within a single day and comparable as given. If they wrapped, I'd normalise to minutes since a fixed origin first.

examples.explanation: Around 11:00–11:20 three trains (the 9:40, 9:50, and 11:00 arrivals) overlap before any of them leaves — the peak is 3.
Each train departs before the next arrives, so they never overlap — one platform suffices.
Both trains are present for the same hour — two platforms required.

approaches.name: Pairwise Overlap Count (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here to anchor the definition — the answer is the peak overlap — then optimise away the quadratic pair comparison.
hints: You need the largest number of trains present at the same time. For one chosen train, how many others are present during its stay?
Two intervals [a1,d1] and [a2,d2] overlap when a1 <= d2 AND a2 <= d1. Count, for each train, how many trains overlap the moment it arrives.
Take the maximum of those counts. That maximum is the minimum number of platforms. It's two nested loops — correct, but O(n²).
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of n trains we scan all n trains to count overlaps at its arrival instant → O(n²) time. We keep only a running max → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Directly count concurrency. For each train `i`, count how many trains are present at the instant train `i` arrives — that is, how many trains `j` satisfy `arr[j] <= arr[i] <= dep[j]` (train `j` arrived at or before `i` and hasn't departed). The maximum of these counts over all `i` is the minimum number of platforms.

**Why the peak occurs at some arrival instant.** Concurrency only ever *increases* at an arrival; departures lower it. So the maximum number of simultaneous trains is reached right when some train arrives, never strictly between events. That means checking the overlap count at each arrival instant is enough — we don't need to test arbitrary times.

**Why the answer is the peak, not the total.** A platform can be reused once a train leaves, so the total number of trains over the day is irrelevant. What forces you to build more platforms is the single busiest instant — the largest pile-up of overlapping intervals. That maximum overlap is exactly the resource you must provision.

**Why we don't ship this.** Counting overlaps by comparing every train against every other is `O(n²)`. For `n = 10⁵` that's `10¹⁰` comparisons — far too slow. The waste is that we recompute overlap from scratch at each arrival. The optimal approach instead processes arrivals and departures in time order and keeps a running balance, so each event is handled once.
approaches.insight: Concurrency rises only at arrivals, so the peak is some arrival instant — that observation is what later lets us sweep events in time order instead of comparing pairs. The O(n²) is purely the cost of recomputing overlaps independently for each train.

pitfalls: Returning the total number of trains instead of the peak overlap.

approaches.name: Sort + Two-Pointer Sweep (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'sort arrivals and departures separately, then sweep a +1/-1 balance in time order'.
hints: The peak overlap changes only at events (an arrival or a departure). What if you processed all events in time order and kept a running count?
Sort arrivals ascending and departures ascending into two separate arrays — you don't need to know which train is which, only how many are present.

Walk both arrays with pointers i (arrivals) and j (departures). If the next arrival is at or before the next departure, a train comes in (count++, update peak); otherwise one leaves (count--). Stop when all arrivals are processed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting the two arrays is O(n log n). The sweep advances i or j every step and stops after the last arrival, so it's O(n). Only a few counters → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the arrival times and the departure times into two separate ascending arrays. Use two pointers, `i` over arrivals and `j` over departures, and a running `platforms` count. At each step compare the next arrival with the next departure: if the arrival is earlier or equal, a train enters (`platforms++`, advance `i`, update the peak); otherwise the earliest still-occupied train leaves (`platforms--`, advance `j`). Continue until every arrival is consumed. The peak `platforms` value is the answer.

**Why decoupling arrivals from departures is legal.** We never care *which* train is on a platform, only *how many* are. So we can sort all arrivals together and all departures together, even though that splits each train's own pair into two different arrays. The merge of these two sorted streams reconstructs the timeline of events in order, which is all the count depends on.

**Why the two-pointer merge gives the right balance.** Sweeping the two sorted arrays in lockstep is a merge: at each moment we handle the chronologically next event. An arrival pushes the concurrent count up; a departure pulls it down. Because concurrency peaks only on arrivals, we check the peak right after each `platforms++`. When the last arrival is processed, no later event can raise the count, so we can stop — remaining departures only lower it.

**Why the tie rule is `arr[i] <= dep[j]`.** If a train arrives at the exact instant another departs and they *cannot* share a platform, the arrival must be counted before the departure frees its slot. Using `<=` processes the arrival first, so the count momentarily includes both — correctly demanding a separate platform. If the problem said they *could* share, you'd flip to `<` (process the departure first).

**Why this is optimal.** Each event is handled exactly once after the sort, so the sweep is linear and sorting dominates. There's no way to know the peak overlap without at least ordering the events, so `O(n log n)` is the natural bound (unless times are small bounded integers, where a difference array hits `O(n + maxTime)`).
approaches.insight: Decoupling each interval's start from its end and sorting them separately is the sweep-line trick: a sorted merge of starts and ends reduces 'maximum overlap' to a running +1/-1 balance. It generalises directly to Meeting Rooms II and any peak-concurrency question.

code.python:
def min_platforms(self, arr: list[int], dep: list[int]) -> int:
    arr.sort()
    dep.sort()
    n = len(arr)
    i = j = 0
    platforms = peak = 0
    while i < n:
        if arr[i] <= dep[j]:
            platforms += 1          # a train arrives
            peak = max(peak, platforms)
            i += 1
        else:
            platforms -= 1          # earliest occupied train leaves
            j += 1
    return peak

java.explanation: Sort the two event streams independently — pairing by train is irrelevant to a count.
Arrival-first tie rule: at equal times the arriving train needs its own platform.
Update peak only on arrivals — that's when concurrency can rise.
Stop once all arrivals are processed; later departures can only lower the count.

python.explanation: Two independent ascending sorts set up the merge sweep.
Next event is an arrival (ties go to arrival) → one more train present.
Record the busiest instant; the final peak is the platform count.

pitfalls: Keeping arrivals paired with their own departures instead of sorting the two arrays separately.
Using arr[i] < dep[j] when the convention says an arrival and a departure at the same time can't share — flips the tie wrongly.
Updating the peak on departures too — harmless to the max but signals a muddled mental model.

commonMistakes: Returning the total number of trains rather than the maximum simultaneous overlap.
Keeping each train's arrival tied to its own departure instead of sorting the two arrays independently.
Mishandling the arr == dep tie so two trains incorrectly share one platform.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting total trains, not peak overlap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Platforms are reusable once a train leaves, so the answer is the busiest instant, not the day's train count. Returning n hugely overestimates.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return len(arr)            # total trains, ignores reuse
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# sweep and track the maximum concurrent count
return peak

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong tie handling
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If an arrival at the same time as a departure cannot share a platform, the arrival must be counted before the departure frees up. Using < processes the departure first and undercounts by one at ties.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting arrivals but reusing original departures
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you sort arr but compare against dep in original order, the departure pointer no longer tracks the earliest still-occupied train and the balance becomes nonsense. Sort BOTH.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
arr.sort()                 # dep left unsorted
# ... compare arr[i] <= dep[j] with unsorted dep
